Running a job that takes hours

John Ehrlinger

Source: vignettes/articles/long-running-jobs.qmd

Most jobs render in a minute or two, and the Render button is fine for them. A Boostmtree fit, a VarPro run or a set of SHAP plots is different. It can run for hours, and over those hours a Workbench session times out, or freezes, or hands you a 502. A render started from that session goes down with it, and so does a background job in RStudio, because both are still attached to the session.

So a long job needs to run on its own, the way nohup runs a command from a terminal. You should not need to know Unix to get that. The functions here do it from the R console, and the job’s own guards send you to them when you forget.

All of this is for Linux and the Workbench. submit_job(), run_job() and cancel_job() are not available on Windows.

Start it 

library(hvtiRtemplates)
job <- "analyses/nb.boostmtree.lvef.boost.qmd"
run_job(job)

run_job() first looks for what would otherwise stop the job minutes or hours in: that this session’s R is the one the study’s renv.lock records, that the packages are installed at the locked versions, that Quarto can be found, that this job is not already running, and that no other job is rendering in the study. It lists every problem it finds, with its fix, and starts nothing until they are cleared.

Then it calls submit_job() and waits up to five minutes (wait = 300) for the render’s own checks. When those have reported, or the wait runs out, you get your console back and the render carries on either way. run_job(job, final = TRUE) is the final render, under the same rules as render_job(job, final = TRUE).

submit_job(job) is the part underneath: it starts the detached render and returns at once, with none of the checks first. Reach for run_job() unless you have a reason not to.

From a terminal, the hvti command does the same on the R the study’s renv.lock records. Install it once with install_hvti("~/bin"), and again after updating the package. Then hvti run, hvti status and hvti cancel take the job’s file, and hvti run <job> --final is the final render.

Come back to it

Close RStudio if you like. A later session starts with nothing loaded, so load the package and name the same file again:

library(hvtiRtemplates)
job <- "analyses/nb.boostmtree.lvef.boost.qmd"
job_status(job)

The first word of the line is the state:

state what it means
none no run is recorded for this job
submitted started, and the render has not reported in yet
running the render is going; see below for what this can and cannot promise
finished done, and the report is beside the job
failed it stopped, and where the log can say, why and fix lines follow
vanished the process went away without recording an end, as a killed one does
cancelled stopped by cancel_job()

Now the question you actually have after two hours: is it still alive, or is it stuck? On the node that started the job, a recorded running is checked against the process itself, so running there means alive. From another node it cannot be checked, and the line says so and names the host. Sessions can land on different nodes, so read that line before you worry.

Alive is not the same as moving, and one long fit can hold a job in a single step for hours. The render records its progress in <job>.run.progress: the chunk it is in, the step within it where the template reports steps, and how long each finished chunk took. job_status() prints that, with an estimate of the time left in the current chunk, and says when nothing has moved for half an hour or more. That is a reason to look, not proof of a hang. The full output is in <job>.run.log, which gets a line as each chunk starts and ends and, within a step, at most every ten minutes.

Stop it 

cancel_job(job)

This stops the render and everything it started, Quarto’s own processes included, and records cancelled, so the job can be submitted again. It is deliberately careful, because the wrong process is easy to hit on a shared server. It leaves alone a process number since reused by something else, and it refuses when it cannot be sure of the process’s identity.

It also refuses a job recorded on another node and names that node, since a process can be signaled only where it runs: open a session there and cancel from it. If that session is gone and you have confirmed the job is not running there, cancel_job(job, other_host = "abandon") records the run as ended without signaling anything. A render still running there would go on writing the job’s output, so do not use it on a guess.

When a job stops you first

Two guards in the templates catch the mistake at the moment it would cost you.

guard_long_fit() sits just before an expensive fit. In the console, or running chunks one by one, with no cached result yet, it stops and tells you to use submit_job(), because the fit would die with your session. A render passes, and so does a cached result, which is why the chunks run interactively once the fit has been done. nb-boostmtree calls it today.

guard_memory() sits at the top of a fit chunk, with the memory the fit is expected to need. It reads your session’s limit and stops, in the first minutes of the render, when the need is over 90 percent of it. The message begins memory: and names the Workbench profile that would hold the fit, and, where the template can work it out, how many cores would fit in this one. A detached job counts against the session that submitted it, so choose the profile before you submit. A fit that outgrows the limit is killed without a message, which is the failure this guard exists to replace.

When it says something is already running

Three things can say this, and they read alike.

One render per study. “Another Quarto render is in progress” is the study’s lock. A study renders one job at a time, whichever job it is, so renaming your job or rendering a copy meets the same lock. Wait for the other render. A lock left by a crash on this node is taken over for you at once. A process on another node cannot be checked from here, so a running render keeps a heartbeat in the lock, and one that has stopped for ten minutes is taken over too. A lock from an older release has no heartbeat and reads as still running. Once you know nothing is rendering on that node, delete the directory the message names.

Another job’s run record. “another job is … in this study”, from run_job(), comes from that job’s record rather than the lock, so deleting the lock does not clear it. The message gives the way out: wait, or stop that job. If it is recorded on another node, check from a session there. Once you have confirmed it has stopped, clear its record with cancel_job(other_job, other_host = "abandon"), as the message prints it.

One submit per job. <job>.run.lock is held while a submit or cancel is in progress. A submit that crashed can leave it behind, and then you delete it to try again.

Errors about a very large file, or about a file Quarto cannot remove from the job’s execute directory, are a different problem that we are still working through with the server’s administrators. These locks do not explain them.
